title: Joshua 23:9–16
context: Joshua continues that the LORD has driven out great nations and fights for Israel, so one Israelite will chase a thousand, and he urges them to love the LORD. He warns that if they turn back, intermarry with the remaining nations, and serve other gods, those nations will become a snare and God will bring on them the evil he threatened, just as every good promise has been fulfilled. Both traditions share the reading of God’s faithfulness in blessing and warning and the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: “For the LORD has driven great and strong nations out from before you. But as for you, no man has stood before you to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has driven out great and strong nations, and no one has stood before Israel. Arminian readers note that Joshua again grounds his appeal in what God has done.

The record of victory is meant to encourage trust, not pride.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s power displayed in Israel’s victories. The nations were stronger, but the LORD fought for his people.

The verse sets up the call to love God in verse 11.

verses.text: One man of you shall chase a thousand; for it is the LORD your God who fights for you, as he spoke to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
One man will chase a thousand, for the LORD fights for them. Arminian readers note the echo of covenant promises (Lev 26:8; Deut 32:30).

The strength is God’s, given to a faithful people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the disproportion as a sign that victory belongs to God.

“As he spoke to you” again ties the outcome to God’s promise rather than to Israel’s numbers or skill.

verses.text: Take good heed therefore to yourselves, that you love the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take good heed therefore to yourselves, that you love the LORD your God.” Arminian readers note that love for God is something the people must guard and cultivate.

The heart of the covenant is love, not mere outward compliance (cf. Deut 6:5).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see love as the heart of covenant obedience (Deut 6:5).

The command calls for vigilance. Reformed readers add that love for God is itself a response to his prior love (cf. 1 John 4:19).

verses.text: “But if you do at all go back, and hold fast to the remnant of these nations, even these who remain among you, and make marriages with them, and go in to them, and they to you;
verses.arminianNotes:
If Israel turns back and intermarries with the remaining nations, the consequences will be grave. Arminian readers note the conditional “if,” which treats falling away as a real possibility for the people.

The concern is spiritual: such unions would draw Israel to other gods (cf. Deut 7:3–4).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the danger of alliances that lead to idolatry (Deut 7:3–4).

The warning is real and serious for the covenant community. The issue is religious allegiance, not ethnicity as such.

verses.text: know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no longer drive these nations from out of your sight; but they shall be a snare and a trap to you, a scourge in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good land which the LORD your God has given you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The nations would become a snare, trap, scourge, and thorns, and God would no longer drive them out. Arminian readers note the vivid images, drawn from earlier warnings (Exod 23:33; Num 33:55).

Judges 2:3 records this warning coming true.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s discipline on covenant unfaithfulness, which Judges 2:3 describes.

The phrase “until you perish from off this good land” shows that the gift of the land could be lost through persistent rebellion.

verses.text: “Behold, today I am going the way of all the earth. You know in all your hearts and in all your souls that not one thing has failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spoke concerning you. All have happened to you. Not one thing has failed of it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua says he is going the way of all the earth, and that not one good thing God promised has failed. Arminian readers note that the people can confirm this from their own hearts and experience (cf. Josh 21:45).

God’s track record invites continued trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a ringing affirmation of God’s faithfulness: “Not one thing has failed of it” (cf. 1 Kings 8:56).

The phrase “the way of all the earth” is also used of David’s approaching death (1 Kings 2:2).

verses.text: It shall happen that as all the good things have come on you of which the LORD your God spoke to you, so the LORD will bring on you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land which the LORD your God has given you,
verses.arminianNotes:
As God fulfilled every good promise, he will also bring the evil things he warned of. Arminian readers note that God’s faithfulness applies to warnings as well as promises.

The covenant blessings and curses are both real (cf. Deut 28).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see God’s faithfulness to his whole word, both promise and threat (Deut 28; Lev 26).

God’s consistency should produce both comfort and holy fear in his people.

verses.text: when you disobey the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods, and bow down yourselves to them. Then the LORD’s anger will be kindled against you, and you will perish quickly from off the good land which he has given to you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
If they disobey the covenant and serve other gods, the LORD’s anger will burn and they will perish from the land. Arminian readers note the clear condition attached to remaining in the land.

The chapter ends with a sober warning, not a guarantee regardless of conduct.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the seriousness of covenant breaking and God’s just anger against idolatry.

The later history of exile shows this warning fulfilled (2 Kings 17:7–18). Both traditions read it as a real warning to God’s people.
